title: Why Each One Should Eat His Own Turtles: Equality in Uncertainty
coreMove: Test any recommendation by asking whether the person shaping the choice will eat the downside if it goes bad.
sourcePressure: The opening fairness test: a person who sells, advises, recommends, or imposes a choice should not be able to hand the downside to someone else while keeping private certainty or upside.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: Flattening the lesson into generic honesty or nice dealing, instead of asymmetry in who knows and who pays.

sourceAnchors.name: Mercury and the turtles
sourceAnchors.detail: The source opens with people who caught and cooked turtles trying to pass the unpleasant meal to Mercury, who forces them to eat what they brought.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: The turtle meal gives the rule its bite: if you brought the exposure into the room, you do not get to serve it to someone else.

sourceAnchors.name: Cicero
sourceAnchors.detail: The source uses Cicero's report of the Rhodes corn problem to ask how much a seller must disclose when he knows more than the buyer.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: The Rhodes merchant matters because the harm begins before the sale, at the point where one side knows the weather and the other side buys the cargo blind.

sourceAnchors.name: Rav Safra
sourceAnchors.detail: The source presents Rav Safra refusing a higher price that arose while he was silently praying because his original intention had already fixed a fairer price.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Rav Safra makes transparency harsher than disclosure: even the seller's silent intention becomes part of the moral ledger.

exampleSpecs.domain: commissioned benefits broker recommending a tax product to a clinic owner

exampleSpecs.stakes: an audit bill could land after the broker has collected commission
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Sarah circles the indemnity clause, asks who pays if the tax treatment fails, and refuses to sign until the broker accepts written downside.
